title: What the model already knows
objectives: Explain why a model's training cut-off is look-ahead, and find the clean test window.

screens.title: A signal that stopped working
screens.prose: A vendor sells a daily sentiment score from a language model. Trading its sign on our seeded market (the generator plants real signal, memory of later returns and late news, each of a known size) gives the P&L below, from January 2016 to September 2023.
screens.question: What most likely changed on 1 October 2021, where the slope breaks?

options.text: The model's training text ends there
The market regime changed that month
options.why: A regime change would not lift the earlier slope to an annual Sharpe near 9; and the planted data has none.

options.text: Trading costs rose sharply
options.why: This P&L has no costs in it at all.

options.text: The strategy's run of luck ended
options.why: Luck does not produce a Sharpe near 9 for six years and then stop on one date.

hints.text: A Sharpe ratio near 9 for six years is not a trading edge anyone has.
Ask what the model could have read about those years.

feedback.correct: The break sits at the model's training cut-off: before it, the scores were partly memory.
feedback.generic: Not quite. What does a language model know about the years it was trained on?

explain.text: Before the cut-off the annualised Sharpe is 9.2; after it, 1.0. The model was trained on text that described those earlier days, including what followed them.

screens.title: How much of the test is clean?
screens.prose: Drag the vendor's stated cut-off along the backtest's dates. Only the days after it test the model's reading; the days before it may test its memory.

state.caption: Share after the cut-off: {{fixed(max(0, min(1, (2023.67 - c.x) / 7.67)), 2)}} (by calendar time)

derive.caption: Share after the cut-off: {{fixed(max(0, min(1, (2023.67 - c.x) / 7.67)), 2)}} (by calendar time)

screens.question: With the cut-off at 1 October 2021, what share of the 2,000 trading days comes after it? Give 2 decimal places.

hints.text: The backtest is 2,000 trading days; the cut-off is trading day 1,500.
Days after it: $2000 - 1500$.

feedback.correct: $500/2000 = 0.25$: a quarter of the backtest tests reading.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Count the trading days after the cut-off and divide by 2,000.

byKey.before: 0.75 is the share before the cut-off, the part that may be memory.

explain.text: Day 1,500 is 1 October 2021, so 500 of 2,000 days, 0.25, are after it. The caption's calendar share is close; counting trading days is exact.

screens.title: The clean window
screens.prose: A model trained on text up to its **training cut-off** may have **memorised** what happened on earlier dates. Only dates after the cut-off form the **clean window**, where a score must come from reading. There the daily P&L has mean 0.0605% and standard deviation 0.9640%.
screens.question: What is the annualised Sharpe ratio in the clean window? Give 2 decimal places.

hints.text: Annualise a daily Sharpe by $\sqrt{252}$.

feedback.generic: Not quite. Divide the mean by the standard deviation, then multiply by the square root of 252.

byKey.daily: That is the daily Sharpe. Multiply by $\sqrt{252}$ to annualise.
byKey.x252: You multiplied by 252. Sharpe ratios scale by the square root of time.

explain.text: $0.0627 \times 15.875 = 1.00$, against 9.22 before the cut-off. The clean figure is the one that measures reading.

screens.title: Before the cut-off
screens.prose: Before the cut-off the daily P&L has mean 0.5058% and standard deviation 0.8711%. The planted memory adds twice the next day's return, in units of its spread, to the score.
screens.question: What is the annualised Sharpe before the cut-off? Give 1 decimal place.

hints.text: Same formula as the last screen.

feedback.correct: About 9.2, more than nine times the clean 1.00.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Mean over standard deviation, times $\sqrt{252}$.

byKey.daily: That is the daily figure; annualise it.

explain.text: 9.2 before against 1.00 after. No real strategy jumps by that much at a model's cut-off; the difference is memory, not skill.

screens.title: Has it seen this document?
screens.prose: A memorisation check from `post-train` level 4: give the model a news story's opening words and compare what it writes back with the story. Count the story's **n-grams** (runs of $n$ words) that appear in the model's text. The story has 16 words; the model's text repeats its first 12.

rows: lenders to corran refused to extend the credit line on friday and the shares fell sharply
lenders to corran refused to extend the credit line on friday and its bonds fell

screens.question: What share of the story's 5-grams appear in the model's text? Give 4 decimal places.

hints.text: A 16-word story has $16 - 5 + 1 = 12$ five-grams.
A 5-gram is shared when all five words sit inside the shared opening of 12 words.
That is $12 - 5 + 1 = 8$ of them.

feedback.generic: Not quite. Count 5-grams that lie inside the 12 shared words.

byKey.three: 0.7143 is the 3-gram share. Longer n-grams are the stricter test.
byKey.words: That counts words. The check counts runs of five words.

explain.text: Eight of the story's twelve 5-grams appear word for word: 0.6667. A model that writes back two thirds of a story's 5-grams has very likely read it; short n-grams match by chance, which is why $n$ of 5 or more is used.

screens.title: A cut-off is a claim
screens.prose: The vendor's documents give the model's training cut-off as 1 October 2021.
screens.question: Why treat that date as a claim to test, not a fact?

options.text: Models are updated after release, and text near the cut-off is thin
Vendors usually lie about dates
options.why: No dishonesty is needed: a later fine-tune or update moves the real cut-off quietly.

options.text: The cut-off is exact, so it needs no test
options.why: Training text near the cut-off is sparse and updates add later text; the boundary is fuzzy.

options.text: It does not matter once you use the clean window
options.why: The clean window is defined by the cut-off, so a wrong cut-off makes the window wrong.

hints.text: What happens to a deployed model after its first release?

feedback.correct: Updates can add later text and the boundary is fuzzy; leave a buffer and check with an overlap test.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Can the real cut-off differ from the stated one?

explain.text: A buffer of a few months after the stated cut-off, and an overlap test on documents from just after it, guard against a fuzzy or moved boundary.

screens.title: Only the news, not the prices
screens.prose: A researcher argues: 'The model was trained on news text, never on price data, so it cannot know the returns.'
screens.question: Why is the backtest before the cut-off still contaminated?

options.text: News after a date describes what prices did, so the model has read the outcomes
It is not: without prices the model cannot leak returns
options.why: News reports say 'shares fell 8% after...'. Reading later news is reading the returns.

options.text: Because news sites also print price tables
options.why: Even without tables, the words 'rallied' or 'collapsed' carry the outcome.

options.text: Because language models are random
options.why: Randomness adds noise; it does not create a Sharpe near 9.

hints.text: What does a news story written the day after a profit warning say?

feedback.correct: Later news is a record of what prices did; a model that read it can score earlier days with hindsight.
feedback.generic: Not quite. What do news stories after an event report?

byKey.safe: You assumed text without prices is safe. Stories after a date report the move itself, so the model has read the returns in words.

explain.text: A story dated after an earnings miss says the shares fell. The model's memory of that story is what gave the planted Sharpe of 9.2 before the cut-off.

screens.title: A cut-off after the sample
screens.prose: A second model's training text runs to March 2024. Our backtest ends in September 2023.
screens.question: What share of the backtest is in its clean window?

hints.text: Is any backtest day after the cut-off?

feedback.correct: None: every day is before the cut-off, so the backtest cannot tell reading from memory.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Compare the backtest's end with the cut-off.

byKey.all: You counted the whole backtest. Every day of it is before this model's cut-off.

explain.text: A model whose cut-off is after the whole sample has no clean window: 0. Only data that arrives after the cut-off can test it, so the test waits.

screens.title: Look-ahead from what a model knows
screens.prose:
What you found, as `fin-ml` level 2's rule applied to a model: a score dated $t$ must not use anything learned after $t$. For a model with cut-off $c$ and a buffer $b$, only dates $t > c + b$ test reading, and the share of the backtest left is

$$\frac{\#\{t : t > c + b\}}{\#\{t\}}.$$
screens.question: A backtest runs 2016 to 2023 and the model's cut-off is 2019. Which result should be quoted?

options.text: The Sharpe after 2019 plus a buffer, and the share it covers
The Sharpe ratio over all eight years
options.why: Five of the eight years may be memory; the full figure mixes them in.

options.text: The Sharpe ratio before 2019, which has more data
options.why: More data of the wrong kind: those years test memory.

options.text: The average of the two periods' Sharpe ratios
options.why: Averaging in memorised years still inflates the result.

hints.text: Which dates can test reading?

feedback.correct: Quote the clean window only, and say how long it is.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Which period can the model not remember?

explain.text: Only the clean window measures reading. Its length matters too: a short window gives a noisy Sharpe, the subject of level 2's last lesson.

widget.prelude:
import numpy as np
from llm_apps_ops_l2 import make_market
import pandas as pd


def _pnl(m):
    D = pd.DataFrame(m['docs'])
    D['published'] = pd.to_datetime(D['published'])
    days = pd.DataFrame({'decision': pd.to_datetime(m['dates']) + pd.Timedelta('16:30:00')})
    J = pd.merge_asof(days, D.sort_values('published'), left_on='decision', right_on='published', direction='backward')
    return np.nan_to_num(np.sign(J['score'].to_numpy()) * m['ret'])

screens.title: Questions for a vendor
screens.prose: A data vendor offers a model-scored news sentiment feed with a backtest from 2012 and a Sharpe ratio of 3. Your desk can trial it for three months.
screens.question: Which question matters most before the trial?

options.text: What is the model's cut-off, and was it retrained?
Can the Sharpe ratio be shown with costs?
options.why: Costs matter, but a backtest scored by a model that has read the period can be wrong by far more than costs.

options.text: How many stocks does the feed cover?
options.why: Coverage is useful, but it cannot tell memory from reading.

options.text: How fast is the feed delivered each morning?
options.why: Speed matters for trading, but first ask whether the backtest is real.

hints.text: Which fact decides how much of the backtest is clean?

feedback.correct: The cut-off (and any retraining) decides which years of the backtest test reading.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Which fact tells memory from reading?

explain.text: Ask for the cut-off and the retraining history, then judge the backtest only on dates after them; the three-month trial is itself a clean window, if a short one.

ideas: A model trained on text up to its cut-off has read what happened after earlier dates, so a backtest before the cut-off can score memory, not reading.
Only the clean window, dates after the cut-off plus a buffer, tests reading; quote its Sharpe and how much of the sample it covers.
A stated cut-off is a claim: models are updated and the boundary is fuzzy, so add a buffer and check suspect documents with an n-gram overlap test.
summary.trap: 'It saw only news, not prices': later news describes the prices.

quiz.question: What is the best reply?

options.text: The news it read after each date reports what prices did
Agreed: no prices means no leak
options.why: Stories report moves in words: 'the shares fell 8%'.

options.text: It probably saw price tables too
options.why: That may be so, but the words alone already carry the outcome.

options.text: Its outputs are random, so it cannot leak
options.why: Randomness does not remove memorised content.

feedback.correct: Later news describes the returns, so reading it is reading the outcomes.
feedback.generic: Not quite. What do news stories after an event report?

explain.text: Text written after a date describes what happened then, prices included, so a model trained on it carries the outcome.
